Use a partial bundle of plotly.js

Source: R/partial_bundles.R
partial_bundle.Rd

Leveraging plotly.js' partial bundles can lead to smaller file sizes and faster rendering. The full list of available bundles, and the trace types that they support, are available here

Usage

partial_bundle(p, type = "auto", local = TRUE, minified = TRUE)

Arguments

p

a go_figure() or htmlwidget.

type

name of the (partial) bundle. The default, 'auto', attempts to find the smallest single bundle that can render p (including the traces of its animation frames). If no single partial bundle can render p, then the full bundle ('full') is used.

local, minified

unused: the bundles are the minified ones shipped with the package, which work without an internet connection (kept for compatibility with the plotly package).

Value

p, which renders with that bundle.

Details

By default, figures load the full plotly.js bundle (about 4.8 MB). The partial bundles shipped with plotly.core (and their trace types) are:

  • "basic": bar, pie, scatter (about 1.2 MB)

  • "cartesian": also box, contour, heatmap, histogram, histogram2d, histogram2dcontour, image, scatterternary, violin

  • "finance": bar, candlestick, funnel, funnelarea, histogram, indicator, ohlc, pie, scatter, waterfall

  • "geo": choropleth, scatter, scattergeo

  • "gl2d": parcoords, scatter, scattergl, splom

  • "gl3d": cone, isosurface, mesh3d, scatter, scatter3d, streamtube, surface, volume

  • "map": choroplethmap, densitymap, scatter, scattermap

Use options(plotly.core.bundle = "auto") to use the smallest bundle for every figure. partial_bundle() is an S3 generic, so packages can add methods for their own figure classes (the plotly package does for plot_ly() objects).

WARNING: use this function with caution when rendering multiple plotly graphs on a single website. That's because a page loads a single plotly.js: if multiple plotly.js bundles are used, one bundle (the full bundle, if any graph uses it) is loaded for all of them, and graphs with trace types it doesn't have won't render. See the examples section for an example.

Author

Carson Sievert

Examples


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# This function is always safe to use when rendering a single
# plotly graph. In this case, we get a 3x file reduction.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
library(plotly.core)
p <- go_figure() |> add_scatter(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, mode = "markers")
save_widget <- function(p, f) {
  write_html(p, f)
  mb <- round(file.info(f)$size / 1e6, 3)
  message("File is: ", mb, " MB")
}
f1 <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
f2 <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
save_widget(p, f1)
save_widget(partial_bundle(p), f2)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# But, since a page loads one plotly.js,
# be careful when putting multiple graphs in a larger document!
# Here the page loads the full bundle, which the surface (part of the
# gl3d bundle, not the cartesian one) needs.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

library(htmltools)
p1 <- go_figure() |>
  add_heatmap(z = volcano) |>
  partial_bundle()
p2 <- go_figure() |>
  add_surface(z = volcano) |>
  partial_bundle(type = "full")
browsable(tagList(plotly_widget(p1), plotly_widget(p2)))
} # }
